faq.q: Why is the PDA often involved in inferior MI?

faq.a: When PCI cannot be performed within 120 min of first medical contact, thrombolysis is the next best option.
faq.q: When is thrombolysis preferred over PCI in low‑resource settings?

exam: What ECG changes confirm a PDA infarction? — ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF; reciprocal depression in I, aVL
Which drug is contraindicated in a patient with active bleeding? — Anticoagulants (e.g., heparin)
What is the first step if a patient with suspected inferior MI develops hypotension? — Assess volume status and start IV fluids; consider thrombolysis
How would you differentiate an inferior MI from pericarditis on ECG? — Inferior MI shows ST elevation in II, III, aVF with PR depression; pericarditis shows diffuse ST elevation and PR depression
Why is a beta‑blocker avoided in a patient with acute pulmonary edema? — It can worsen hypotension and reduce cardiac output
What is the most common complication of an inferior MI in a low‑resource setting? — Ventricular septal rupture or papillary muscle rupture leading to acute heart failure
ai.title: Posterior Descending Artery
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The posterior descending artery (PDA) supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle and posterior septum. In low‑resource settings, its occlusion presents as an inferior myocardial infarction with limited diagnostic tools. Clinicians must recognise clinical patterns and use bedside tests to guide urgent reperfusion.

sections.p: The PDA is the distal branch of the right coronary artery in most adults, running in the posterior interventricular groove. It supplies the inferior LV wall and part of the conduction system. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by ECG changes and, where available, cardiac enzymes.

t.b: Shows ST‑segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF indicating inferior MI – confirms PDA territory involvement
Elevated levels confirm myocardial necrosis; a rise >3× upper limit suggests significant infarction
May show pulmonary congestion if heart failure develops; not specific for PDA

b: Severe: marked pain, hypotension, arrhythmia, heart failure
sections.p: Inferior MI severity is graded by extent of ST elevation, enzyme rise, and clinical symptoms. In low‑resource settings, a simple classification: mild (ST 1–2 mm), moderate (2–5 mm), severe (>5 mm).

The leading cause is atherosclerotic plaque rupture in the PDA. In East Africa, additional contributors include rheumatic heart disease, HIV‑associated vasculitis, and high prevalence of smoking and hypertension.

b: Right‑sided heart failure signs (leg edema, jugular venous distension)
sections.p: Patients report crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm or jaw, often with diaphoresis. Inferior MI may present with syncope, dizziness, or right‑sided heart failure signs. In low‑resource settings, symptoms may be vague and delayed.

b: Bedside ultrasound – detect pericardial effusion or LV dysfunction
sections.p: Bedside ECG and troponin are essential. When unavailable, clinical assessment and pulse oximetry guide urgency. Chest X‑ray and bedside ultrasound can detect complications.

t.b: Detects ST elevation in inferior leads – confirms PDA infarction
Elevated levels confirm myocardial injury – guides reperfusion urgency
Shows LV dysfunction or pericardial effusion – indicates complications

sections.p: Urgent red flags include hypotension, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, or new heart failure. Complications may involve ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, or arrhythmias.

Immediate management focuses on reperfusion (thrombolysis or PCI if available), antiplatelet therapy, anticoagulation, and supportive care. In low‑resource settings, streptokinase or tenecteplase may be used if PCI is unavailable.

After stabilization, patients need secondary prevention: lifestyle modification, control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and smoking cessation. Follow‑up includes ECG, echocardiography, and repeat troponin if symptoms recur.

b: Pericarditis – diffuse ST elevation, PR depression
sections.p: Inferior MI can mimic right‑sided heart failure, pulmonary embolism, or pericarditis. Distinguishing features include ECG changes and the presence of ST elevation in inferior leads.

b: Ultrasound – small effusion may be missed
sections.p: Troponin can be falsely normal early; ECG may be normal in the first hour. Bedside ultrasound may miss small effusions. Clinicians should repeat tests if suspicion remains high.

whenToSeekHelp: Hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiogenic shock, new heart failure, sudden worsening pain
